opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I've been thinking about a lot lately, because I think there's a hidden issue that people tend to overlook. We usually judge these models by their outputs. If the output is good, if it passes the benchmark, we assume that whatever is going on inside must be fine. But two systems can produce exactly the same output and have completely different internal representations, and that difference really matters when you ask what they can do *next*.

The way I'd put it is that the representations in a lot of current models are what you might call fractured and entangled. They get to the right answer, but the underlying structure isn't organized in a way that reflects the actual regularities of the world. Things that should be unified are split into separate pieces, and things that should be independent are tangled together. It's a bit like a student who memorized a huge number of special cases rather than understanding the principle. On the test you can't tell them apart, but if you ask them to go somewhere new, the difference shows up right away.

Creativity depends heavily on that. A creative leap isn't random. It's usually taking a deep regularity you understand and pushing it in a direction nobody has pushed it before. If your representation actually captures that regularity, say symmetry, or some modular decomposition of the problem, then small changes to it lead to meaningful, coherent variations. You can explore the space in a sensible way. If the representation is fractured, small changes lead to incoherent or degenerate results, and the space of interesting nearby ideas is basically closed off to you.

We saw this pretty vividly in some of our older work on Picbreeder, where people evolved images through an open-ended process with no particular objective. When you look inside the networks that came out of that, the representations are remarkably elegant. You'll find a single dimension that controls something like a mouth opening and closing, or a skull's shape changing smoothly. That happened because the process wasn't driven toward a fixed target. It accumulated stepping stones that were interesting in their own right, and that seems to produce well-factored, modular structure almost as a byproduct. When you train a network with SGD to reproduce the same image directly, you get the same picture but a much messier inside, and it doesn't support those meaningful variations.

So my worry is that by optimizing so aggressively toward objectives, whether it's next-token prediction or benchmark scores, we may be getting systems that are impressive at interpolating within what they've seen but structurally handicapped at real invention. Scale can paper over a lot of that, because with enough data you cover so many cases that the fractures are hard to see. But the frontier of creativity is exactly where you've run out of cases to cover.

I don't think this is hopeless. It suggests we should pay much more attention to *how* representations form, not just whether the loss goes down. And it suggests that open-ended processes, ones that value interestingness and divergence rather than just convergence on a target, may matter not only for what they discover but for the kind of internal understanding they leave behind. That's the part I find most exciting, and honestly most underexplored.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think this is actually one of the most underappreciated issues in the whole field right now, so I'm glad you're asking about it. The way I'd frame it is that the representations these models learn are fundamentally shaped by the objective, and the objective is prediction. You're trying to get the next token right, you're trying to minimize a loss. And what that does is it produces representations that are, let's say, entangled. They work, they get the job done, but they aren't factored in a way that reflects the actual underlying structure of the world or of the problem.

I've been talking about this in terms of what I call fractured, entangled representations versus unified, factored ones. If you look at something like the picbreeder networks, where humans were doing open-ended search without any particular objective, you'd find that the internal representations ended up being incredibly clean. There'd be a single node that controlled symmetry, or one that controlled the mouth opening on a face. The representation had discovered the actual regularities. Whereas when you train a network with SGD to reproduce the exact same image, you get something that looks right on the outside but inside it's a mess. It's spaghetti. There's no node you can point to and say, this is what it means.

And why does that matter for creativity? Because creative leaps are about recombination and extrapolation. If you want to take an idea and move it in a new direction, you need to have the right handles to grab onto. If the thing you learned about symmetry is smeared across ten thousand weights in a way that's tangled up with color and position and everything else, then you can't cleanly vary it. You can only interpolate within the space of things you've already seen. You can produce things that are superficially novel, sort of a blend, but the kind of leap where someone sees a deep structural analogy between two distant domains, that requires having actually isolated the structure.

So my concern is that the current paradigm produces models that are extraordinarily capable in the sense of having absorbed an enormous amount, but the way they've absorbed it may actually be hostile to the kind of open-ended creative divergence that we associate with real discovery. It's not that they can't be creative at all. It's that the creativity is bounded by a representation that was never built to support it. The representation was built to minimize loss, and those are just different things.

And I'd add, this is why I keep coming back to open-endedness and divergence rather than optimization. Nature didn't get to brains by setting an objective. It got there by exploring, by collecting stepping stones that weren't aimed at anything in particular. And the representations that come out of that kind of process seem to be the ones that are actually good for building on. So if we want systems that can make genuine leaps, I think we have to take seriously the idea that how you got the representation matters as much as what it can do on a benchmark.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is whether the representation lets you see a stepping stone that you weren’t looking for. A representation isn’t just a way of storing what you know. It determines which things look similar, which differences matter, and which possibilities you can even recognize.

If you train a system to get very good at a particular objective, it can learn to discard distinctions that don’t help with that objective. That makes sense for solving the task. But something that looks irrelevant today might be precisely what enables a creative leap tomorrow. You can become very competent within a particular framing while losing opportunities to discover a different framing.

That doesn’t mean current models can’t be creative. They can have very rich representations. But I’d distinguish producing a surprising combination from sustaining a process of discovery where what matters changes along the way. Can the system encounter something unexpected, recognize that it’s interesting without already knowing what it’s good for, and pursue it? To me, that’s where representation and open-endedness meet. It’s not only about what the model can express; it’s also about whether its process gives unexpected possibilities somewhere to go.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is whether the representation makes a new possibility accessible at all. We tend to think of creativity as searching harder, but if your representation doesn’t contain the right building blocks, searching harder may not help. Something that looks like a small step from one perspective can be almost impossible to express from another.

Now, learned representations are powerful precisely because we don’t have to specify those building blocks ourselves. But they’re still shaped by the data and by what the model was rewarded for doing. If everything is organized around predicting familiar patterns, some departures from those patterns may be much easier to discover than others.

That connects to this idea of stepping stones. An intermediate discovery might be valuable because of what it makes possible later, even though it doesn’t look like progress toward any particular goal. If the learning process continually discards those deviations, you can lose the path to something creative before you even recognize that there was a path.

So I wouldn’t say that current models can’t be creative. I’d ask whether they can keep developing their representations through exploration, including exploration whose usefulness isn’t apparent in advance. The representation is a constraint, but changing the representation can itself be the creative leap.
